title: Fecal metaproteome profiles of celiac disease patients with poly-autoimmunity
projectDescription: Twenty-eight subjects were selected for the study from among celiac disease patients regularly followed at the Medical Clinic of the University of Sassari. Celiac disease (CD) was diagnosed according to international guidelines. Patients were divided into two groups of 14 subjects based on the presence or absence of additional autoimmune diseases. Only autoimmune diseases confirmed by a specialist's certification were considered for the study. Further inclusion criteria included a body mass index (BMI) between 18 and 25 kg/m², a gluten-free diet (GFD) duration of one year or more, and an age between 18 and 60 years. Exclusion criteria were: (i) use of antibiotics, probiotics, or prebiotics in the 3 months prior to enrollment; (ii) a vegetarian or vegan diet; (iii) a history of malignancy, pregnancy, alcohol abuse, or drug addiction. Following a clinical evaluation, each patient provided a fecal sample. Additionally, three questionnaires were collected concerning: i) anamnestic and anthropometric data, ii) gastrointestinal symptoms, and iii) dietary habits and lifestyle.
sampleProcessingProtocol: An aliquot of 100 to 200 mg of feces was weighed for each sample and resuspended in an extraction buffer composed of 2% SDS, 100 mM dithiothreitol, and 20 mM Tris-HCl at pH 8.8, and incubated at 95°C for 20 minutes in a thermal shaker. After adding a 5 mm diameter steel bead to each sample, the samples were sequentially incubated at -80°C for 10 minutes, subjected to mechanical homogenization by the beads for 10 minutes (30 cycles/s), incubated first at -80°C for 10 minutes and then at 95°C for another 10 minutes, subjected again to homogenization cycles for 10 minutes (30 cycles/s), and finally centrifuged at 20,000 × g for 10 minutes. At the end, the supernatant containing the protein extract was recovered. The protein extracts were then processed according to a modified filter-assisted sample preparation (FASP) digestion protocol. The extracts were diluted with a UA solution (8 M urea in 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.8), loaded onto an Amicon Ultra-0.5 filtration device (30 kDa cutoff), and centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 15 minutes. Sequentially added to the protein extracts were: 200 µL of UA solution, 100 µL of 50 mM iodoacetamide in UA solution, 100 µL of UA solution, an additional 100 µL of UA solution, and 100 µL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate; each dilution was followed by centrifugation at 14,000 × g. Finally, trypsin (1 µg in a 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate solution) was added to each sample, followed by overnight incubation at 37°C. The peptide mixtures were collected by centrifugation; a final elution was also performed with 100 µL of elution solution (20% acetonitrile, 0.2% formic acid). The peptide mixtures were concentrated, resuspended in 0.2% formic acid, and quantified using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. The resulting peptide mixtures were analyzed by LC-MS/MS using a Q-Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer, operating with an EASY-spray source, interfaced with an Easy-nLC 1000 LC system. Peptide mixtures were concentrated and desalted using StageTips. Then, peptides were separated by LC with a C18 EASY-spray column at 35°C with a flow rate of 250 nL/min for 135 min, using the following three-step gradient of eluent B (0.2% formic acid in 95% acetonitrile) in eluent A (0.2% formic acid in 5% acetonitrile): 1-30% for 115 min, 30-60% for 10 min and 60-95% for 10 min. The mass spectrometer was set up in a data dependent MS/MS mode, where a full scan spectrum (from 300 to 1,700 m/z) was followed by MS/MS spectra. After ion activation/dissociation, the 12 most abundant peaks were measured with higher energy C-trap dissociation at a normalized collision energy of 25%. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s and nitrogen was used as collision gas.
dataProcessingProtocol: MS spectra were subjected to bioinformatic analysis using the Proteome Discoverer platform from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Peptide identification was carried out using two different databases in parallel, namely a collection of human gut metagenomes for the microbial part and the Homo sapiens reference proteome for the human part, with SEQUEST-HT as the search engine and Percolator for the statistical validation of identifications. The area of the chromatographic peak associated with each individual peptide was considered a measure of abundance. Peptides were taxonomically annotated with Unipept Desktop (v.1.2.6), while functional annotation was performed at the protein level with the eggNOG-mapper web application, using information from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database.

title: Metaproteomic analysis of paired fresh, frozen and swab-collected/preservation medium-stored feces from four healthy human subjects
projectDescription: Metaproteomic analysis of paired fresh, frozen and swab-collected/preservation medium-stored feces from four healthy human subjects
sampleProcessingProtocol:
Four healthy volunteers (two males and two females) provided a fecal sample and self-collected three aliquots from it. A first aliquot (named eNAT) was collected using a disposable sterile swab and stored at room temperature for 14 days in the stabilizing medium-containing tube provided with the swab (eNAT® 608CS01R device; Copan, Brescia, Italy). According to the manual published by the manufacturer, the eNAT® stabilizing medium contains guanidine thiocyanate, Tris-EDTA, HEPES and an (unspecified) detergent. Two further aliquots were collected from the same fecal sample using the spatula of a disposable sterile stool container (Coprotainer®, Futurlab, Limena, Italy) and stored in the stool container itself; the first of them was processed within one hour of collection (fresh feces, named FF), whereas the second was transferred within one hour of collection in an ultrafreezer (-80°C, named F-80) and stored there for 14 days.
After 14 days of room-temperature storage, eNAT samples were vortexed for 2 min to resuspend the fecal material in the 1 ml of stabilizing medium. The fecal suspensions were then transferred into clean tubes and separated by centrifugation (for 15 min at 16,000 x g) into two phases: a lysis supernatant (eNAT-LS; approximate volume: 1 ml), expected to contain soluble human proteins and microbial proteins come into solution upon cell lysis, and a residual pellet (eNAT-RP; approximate average weight: 100 mg), expected to contain insoluble fecal material and unlysed cells.
An aliquot of each eNAT-LS sample was concentrated and purified through protein precipitation with trichloroacetic acid (TCA) and acetone (named eNAT-LS-PP). Specifically, 250 μl of a 20% TCA solution was added to an equal volume of eNAT-LS, mixed by inversion, and incubated for 30 min on ice. After centrifugation at 16,000 x g for 15 min at 4°C, supernatants were removed and 250 μl of cold acetone was added. Samples were then vortexed for 1 min, incubated for 2 hours at -20°C and centrifuged at 16,000 x g for 10 min at 4°C. After removing the supernatants, protein pellets were resuspended in 100 μl of solubilization buffer (8 M urea, 20 mM DTT, 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.5).
In parallel, eNAT-RP samples were subjected to protein extraction as follows. After adding a 5-mm steel bead (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) and the extraction buffer (2% SDS, 100 mM DTT, 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.5, with 2 μl of buffer added per mg of fecal pellet), samples were incubated at 95°C for 10 min at 500 rpm using a Fisherbrand™ Isotemp™ Cooling Shake Touch Shaker (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA), homogenized for 10 min at 2 m/s using a Fisherbrand™ Bead Mill 24 Homogenizer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and centrifuged for 10 min at 16,000 x g. At the end, the supernatants (i.e., the protein extracts, named eNAT-RP-PE) were collected and stored at -20°C until further analyses.
To process FF and F-80 samples, a fragment of approximately 250 mg was collected and weighed from each fecal sample stored in stool containers (with frozen F-80 samples having been adequately thawed on ice before aliquoting). A preliminary washing step was performed to remove hydrophilic contaminants and interferents, by adding 1 ml of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, USA, now part of Merck) and resuspending the fecal fragments by vortexing for 2 min. After centrifugation (for 15 min at 16,000 x g), two phases were obtained: a washing supernatant (named FF-WS and F-80-WS for the two types of fecal sample, respectively), expected to contain soluble human proteins and hydrophilic interferents, and a fecal pellet (named FF-FP and F-80-FP for the two types of fecal sample, respectively; approximate average weight: 240 mg). WS samples were collected and stored at -20°C; FP samples were subjected to protein extraction, following the same protocol described above for eNAT-RP samples and eventually obtaining the protein extracts (named FF-FP-PE and F-80-FP-PE for the two types of fecal sample, respectively). 
Based on the SDS-PAGE results and other technical considerations, eNAT-LS-PP, FF-FP-PE and F-80-FP-PE (hereafter simplified as eNAT, FF and F-80, respectively) samples were selected for further analyses and then processed according to a modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) protocol. Protein mixtures (15 and 30 μl for FF/FF-80 and eNAT samples, respectively) were diluted to 500 μl with a dilution solution (8M urea, 100 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.5), loaded onto Amicon® Ultra-0.5 filters (30 kDa cutoff; Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) and centrifuged for 15 min at 14,000 x g. Then, 200 μl of dilution solution, 100 μl of 50 mM iodoacetamide (in dilution solution), 100 μl of dilution solution (two times) and 100 μl of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate were sequentially added to the samples, followed by centrifugation for 10 min at 14,000 x g. Finally, 1 μg of trypsin (in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate solution) was added to each sample, followed by incubation at 37°C overnight. Peptide mixtures were eluted in two steps: by a first centrifugation (15 min at 14,000 x g) and then by adding 100 μl of elution solution (20% acetonitrile, 0.5% formic acid) and centrifuging again. Peptide mixtures were finally brought to dryness using a Concentrator Plus (Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany).
Reconstituted peptide mixtures (approximately 5 µg) were purified by SCX StageTips, eluted in 10 µl of 500 mM ammonium acetate containing 20% acetonitrile, then evaporated to dryness and resuspended in 0.2% formic acid. LC was performed on an EasyLC 1200 instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The nanoLC column was a pulled capillary, 0.075x160 mm (i.d. and column length, respectively), in-house packed with C18 silica particles (Dr. Maisch, Ammerbuch, Germany). Peptides were loaded at 500 nl/min in mobile phase A (2% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) and eluted at 300 nl/min by the following gradient: from 0% B to 25% B (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) in 60 min, from 25% B to 45% B in additional 10 minutes, then to 100% B in 8 minutes. The column was regenerated for 10 min at 100% B and equilibrated at 0% B for 20 min before the following injection. Two blank injections were performed in between samples. A shorter gradient (45 min) was utilized for blank injections. Peptides were electrosprayed in positive ion mode using 1800 V as spray voltage into an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Internal calibration was automatically performed at the beginning of each run (RunStart Easy IC-on). Full scan MS parameters were: scan range 375-1400 m/z, resolution 60,000, RF lens 40%, AGC target 100%, maximum injection time 50 msec. Data-dependent acquisition was performed using the following parameters: dependent scans 15 (top-15), dynamic exclusion 20 sec, charge states 2-6, intensity threshold 5e4. Tandem mass spectrometry scans were acquired as follows: isolation window 1.6 m/z, resolution 30,000, normalized collision energy 30%, AGC target 100%, maximum injection time 120 msec.
dataProcessingProtocol: Peptide identification was performed using the Proteome Discoverer™ software (v.2.5; Thermo Fisher Scientific), with Sequest-HT as search engine and Percolator for peptide validation, setting the false discovery rate (FDR) threshold to 1%. Search parameters were as follows: precursor mass range 350-5000 Da; minimum peak count 6; S/N Threshold 2; enzyme trypsin (full); maximum missed cleavage sites 2; peptide length range 5-50 amino acids; precursor mass tolerance 10 ppm; fragment mass tolerance 0.02 Da; static modification cysteine carbamidomethylation; dynamic modification methionine oxidation. Searches were conducted in parallel against two sequence databases, namely a collection of human gut metagenomes and the Homo sapiens reference proteome retrieved from UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (release 2021_04); proteins were categorized as 'microbial' or 'human' when belonging to the first or second database, respectively. Proteins were grouped by the Proteome Discoverer algorithm according to strict parsimony principle, then selecting a representative master protein for each protein group. Offline mass recalibration and label-free MS1 quantitation were carried out using the Spectrum Files RC and the Minora Feature Detector nodes, respectively. Optimal settings for retention time and mass tolerance windows were calculated by the Minora algorithm based on mass accuracy and retention time variance distribution. A consensus feature list was defined based on Feature Mapper and Precursor Ions Quantifier nodes outputs. MS1 signals of all peptides significantly matching with at least an MS2 spectrum from at least one sample were mapped across runs and quantified by calculating the integrated area of the chromatographic peak. Master protein abundances were calculated as the sum of the abundances of all peptides matching that protein sequence. Master protein sequences were annotated using the eggNOG-mapper web application (v.2.1.9, available at http://eggnog-mapper.embl.de/), keeping default parameters and then choosing Cluster of Orthologous Groups (COG) and KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) orthology (KO) information as main functional classifications. The taxonomic annotation provided by eggNOG-mapper was only used at the protein level; peptide taxonomic annotation was instead carried out using Unipept Desktop (v.2.0.0), selecting the three available options ("equate I and L", "filter duplicate peptides" and "advanced missed cleavage handling"). Taxonomic annotations were slightly different between protein and peptide data (e.g., the two synonymic variants Bacteroidota and Bacteroidetes) since updates in taxonomic nomenclature have been adopted after varying periods of time by the different tools. Meta4P (v.1.5.2) was finally employed to parse identification, quantification and annotation data and to calculate the related metrics.

title: Enhancing Peptide Identification in Metaproteomics through Curriculum Learning in Deep Learning
projectDescription: Metaproteomics offers a powerful window into the active functions of microbial communities, but accurately identifying peptides remains challenging due to the size and incompleteness of protein databases derived from metagenomes. These databases often contain vastly more sequences than those from single organisms, creating a computational bottleneck in peptide-spectrum match (PSM) filtering. Here we present WinnowNet, a deep learning–based method for PSM filtering, available in two versions: one using transformers and the other convolutional neural networks. Both variants are designed to handle the unordered nature of PSM data and are trained using a curriculum learning strategy that moves from simple to complex examples. WinnowNet consistently achieves more true identifications at equivalent false discovery rates compared to leading tools, including Percolator, MS$^2$Rescore, and DeepFilter, and outperforms filters integrated into popular analysis pipelines. It also uncovers more gut microbiome biomarkers related to diet and health, highlighting its potential to support advances in personalized medicine
sampleProcessingProtocol: For the ProteomeTools dataset, dried peptide pools were solubilized in 100% DMSO to a concentration of 10 pmol/ul by vortexing for 30 minutes at room temperature, then diluted to 10% DMSO with 1% formic acid in HPLC-grade water. Approximately 200 fmol of each peptide was analyzed using a Dionex 3000 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The LC system was directly coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Each peptide pool was analyzed with a full MS scan in the Orbitrap at a resolution of 60,000, followed by HCD MS/MS scans at 28% normalized collision energy (resolution 15,000), and CID scans at 35% normalized collision energy. For the marine and soil datasets, peptide samples were loaded into the column using a pressure cell. The column was equilibrated with HPLC Solvent A (5% acetonitrile, 95% H2O, 0.1% formic acid), followed by separation on an analytical column containing 15~cm of C18 RP media. Mass spectrometry analysis was performed using an LTQ Orbitrap Elite instrument (Thermo Scientific). Tandem mass spectra were acquired across 11 consecutive online SCX fractions, with MS1 and MS2 scans recorded at resolutions of 30000 and 15000, respectively. For the human gut dataset, fecal samples were suspended in 45mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), vortexed for 45 minutes, and centrifuged at 500 xg for 5 minutes to remove food debris. Proteins were extracted, alkylated with iodoacetamide (IAA), and digested overnight with trypsin. The resulting peptides were purified and concentrated using Pierce C18 spin columns (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and quantified via the Pierce Quantitative Colorimetric Peptide Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were analyzed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a Nano ACQUITY UPLC system. Full MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 120000, followed by HCD MS/MS scans at a resolution of 30000.
dataProcessingProtocol: The MS data was searched using Comet, MS-GF+, Myrimatch and filtered by Percolator, MS2Rescore, Q-ranker, PeptideProphet, iProphet, DeepFilter and WinnowNet. The precursor and fragment mass tolerances were set to 0.09 Da and 0.01 Da, respectively. Peptides within the mass range of 700 to 7000 Da were considered. Trypsin/P was selected as the proteolytic enzyme, with a maximum allowance of three missed cleavages.
